t: LeetCode 1835 — Find XOR Sum of All Pairs Bitwise AND
o:
## Understanding the problem

The XOR sum of a list is the XOR of all its elements. Given two arrays arr1 and arr2 of non-negative integers, form the list of arr1[i] AND arr2[j] over every pair (i, j) and return its XOR sum.

**Example walkthrough:** For arr1 = [1,2,3] and arr2 = [6,5], the six ANDs are [0,1,2,0,2,1]; XOR-ing them, each of 1 and 2 appears twice and cancels itself, leaving 0. For arr1 = [12] and arr2 = [4] there is a single pair, so the answer is simply 12 AND 4 = 4.

With up to 10^5 elements per array, the pairwise list can hold 10^10 entries — enumerating it is hopeless. Values stay below 10^9, i.e., under 2^30, hinting that a per-bit argument or a purely algebraic identity collapses the double loop into a single linear pass.
k: AND distributes over XOR bitwise: (a AND b) XOR (a AND c) = a AND (b XOR c).
Applying that identity across both arrays collapses everything: answer = (XOR of all arr1) AND (XOR of all arr2).
Bit-level view: result bit b is set iff (#arr1 elements with bit b) × (#arr2 elements with bit b) is odd.

a.i: Compute every pair's AND and accumulate with XOR exactly as the statement describes. Correct by construction, but it visits n·m pairs — up to 10^10 at max constraints.
s: For each a in arr1 and each b in arr2, update res ^= a & b.
a.t: O(n · m) — every one of up to 10^10 pairs is visited; far beyond limits.

a.i: Handle each of the 30 bits independently. Pair (i, j) contributes bit b to the grand XOR iff both elements have bit b set; since XOR cancels equal contributions in twos, bit b survives in the answer iff the product of the two per-array set-bit counts is odd.
s: For each bit b from 0 to 29:
Count c1 = number of arr1 elements with bit b set, and c2 likewise for arr2.
If c1 * c2 is odd, set bit b in the result.
a.t: O(30 · (n + m)) — constant number of linear sweeps over both arrays per bit.

a.n: Approach 3: Algebraic identity, XOR-fold then AND (optimal)
a.i: Fold XOR over each array first. By distribution, XOR over j of (arr1[i] AND arr2[j]) equals arr1[i] AND (XOR of arr2); repeating over i leaves (XOR of arr1) AND (XOR of arr2). Two accumulators, one pass per array — verify on Example 1: 1^2^3 = 0, 6^5 = 3, and 0 & 3 = 0.
s: Compute x1 = XOR of every element of arr1.
Compute x2 = XOR of every element of arr2.
a.t: O(n + m) — a single XOR fold over each array.

w:
## Wrap-up

Go straight to the closed-form identity in an interview, but derive it live on one bit position — the derivation IS the solution: fixing a, the map b -> a & b is linear over GF(2), so (a&b) ^ (a&c) = a&(b^c), which lets you fold either array first.

**Common pitfalls:** assuming the same algebra transfers to OR — it does not, since (a|b) ^ (a|c) differs from a|(b^c); miscounting the needed bit width (values up to 10^9 fit in 30 bits); and in the parity approach, overflowing 32-bit counters via c1*c2 in languages without 64-bit promotion care (Java/C++ need long/long long or an odd/even boolean).

**Likely follow-ups:** extend to three arrays, where the answer generalizes neatly to xor(arr1) & xor(arr2) & xor(arr3); handle streaming inputs by folding incrementally; or replace AND with OR/XOR variants and re-derive which identities survive.
